extracted.intended_audience: researchers in mathematical analysis and experimental optics (mathematicians and physicists)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles for assessing theoretical mathematical developments (series, logarithms, multivalued functions) and experimental optics investigations (reflected light, prism/oil experiments). Emphasizes convergence, domain validity, notation, experimental controls, and data reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justify introduction of arbitrary constants (c)
rubrics_metrics.description: The constant c might appear needlessly introduced, but its necessity to insure the convergence (and universal accuracy) of the series is plain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When introducing arbitrary constants into analytical formulae, justify their role explicitly (e.g., ensuring convergence or universal accuracy). Discuss consequences if the constant were omitted and show how it secures required limiting behavior (e.g., (1 - θ c)^n → 0 as n→∞).

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyse series convergence and truncation error
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiate n terms of the series and examine the resulting expression; to learn how far a development is applicable, ascertain the error committed upon calculating n terms and, supposing n an infinitely great integer, observe if any variable values prevent the error expression from vanishing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide an explicit error term for truncated series, study its limit as the number of terms increases, and identify variable ranges where the error fails to vanish. Use this to delimit the domain of numerical validity and to justify taking limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: State domain of applicability of series expansions
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorems of development (Taylor’s, Maclaurin’s, etc.) are based upon hypothetical reasoning; a function may be developable only for values of x between certain limits, and expansions can be illusory outside those limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly declare the interval/region where an expansion is valid. Avoid equating developments that are valid on different domains without demonstrating overlap; flag when equating such expansions can lead to partly or entirely false conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer numerical identity checks in addition to analytic reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: There was some confusion in asserting universally that equations were analytically true which, numerically considered, were in particular instances palpably false; in ascertaining correctness of conclusions one often appeals to numerical identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complement formal algebraic derivations with numerical checks (examples, substitution of representative values) to detect cases where algebraic equivalence does not imply numerical identity in given domains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of conclusions from diverging or illusory series
rubrics_metrics.description: Instances occur where developments, upon substituting a particular value for the variable, show no approximation to numerical identity; diverging series can be dangerous even when final development is converging (Poisson examples).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and avoid using diverging expansions as justification for conclusions unless additional justification is provided. Discuss known counterexamples and cite prior warnings; treat such uses with caution, at minimum noting limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for multivaluedness and independence of numerator/denominator
rubrics_metrics.description: When an expression is required to assume particular values there needs be no correspondence between the numerator and denominator; any value of the formula satisfies the criterion, and numerator and denominator may be wholly independent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When working with multivalued functions (logarithms, roots), state how choices of branches/values are made and ensure arguments respect possible independence between components; avoid implicitly assuming paired correspondence unless proved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use consistent, unambiguous notation for exponentials and logarithms
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism of confusing notation (e.g., varying the meaning of ax according to form of x) and recommendation to adopt the usual interpretation identifying a^x with f(x f^-1 a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define operational meaning of notations like a^x and log_a explicitly, especially when extending definitions beyond integer exponents or to complex/negative arguments. Avoid ad hoc conventions that change symbol meaning depending on context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate real and imaginary parts; specify branch/arc choices
rubrics_metrics.description: To separate the real and imaginary parts of f^-1 θ, inspect arcs on the unit circle and choose the arc/cosine signs depending on semicircle; give expressions that separate real and imaginary parts (see [28]).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When presenting complex-valued inverses (logarithms, inverse trig), give formulas that explicitly separate real and imaginary components and explain branch choices (which semicircle, sign conventions) so readers can reproduce the selected values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define and explain order and rank for multilevel logarithms
rubrics_metrics.description: Indicate order of a logarithm by the z in the denominator and the rank it bears in that order by the z in the numerator; demonstrate that a quantity can have an infinite number of orders and logs in each order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When introducing novel conceptual constructs (e.g., orders and ranks of logarithms), provide clear definitions, illustrative examples, and explain how these relate to traditional concepts; state the novelty and its implications explicitly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design experiments with substitution across materials and configurations
rubrics_metrics.description: Experiments were extended to many mixed oils, soft solids, gums, resins, and prisms of different glass which give similar results; substituted prisms and various minerals were examined to test phenomena across refractive powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test hypotheses across a broad set of materials and experimental configurations to establish generality. Report substitutions made and whether results were consistent, noting any dependence on material properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematically vary and control experimental parameters (angle, temperature, film)
rubrics_metrics.description: Measured angles of incidence on prism surfaces, observed color changes with angle; applied heat to oils to diminish refractive power and recorded changes in brightness and angle at which periods complete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and control key parameters (angles of incidence, temperature, film thickness). Systematically vary single factors while holding others steady to determine causal effects and report measurement procedures and ranges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify experiments and observations into distinct phenomenon classes
rubrics_metrics.description: Experiments divided into two classes: (I) those establishing reflecting forces at confines of media of same refractive power; (II) those producing periodical colours at confines of particular kinds of glass and fluids.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize empirical results by phenomenon type, making it clear which experiments support which classes of conclusions. Use this classification to structure interpretation and avoid conflating distinct effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure spectral dependence (wavelength-specific maxima/minima)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provided periods for red and blue light (first and second minima) and observed how tints and period angles differ between red and blue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report wavelength-dependent measurements (e.g., separate red/blue results), give numerical values for minima/maxima, and discuss how spectral differences inform theoretical interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide physical/graphical models to interpret data
rubrics_metrics.description: Explained results by hypothesizing curves representing reflecting forces in solid and fluid (Figures 2–6) and discussed cases where curves extend to different distances or vary according to different laws to explain observed reflections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complement experimental data with theoretical models or diagrams showing hypothesized mechanisms. Explicitly link model features to observed data and discuss alternative model geometries and their expected signatures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discuss alternative hypotheses and reconcile experiments with competing assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Considered hypothesis where refracting forces vary with same curves as reflecting forces and argued how experiments could be reconciled with mutual dependence; emphasized plausibility and limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When interpreting results, present and evaluate alternative explanations. Explain how data support or contradict competing hypotheses, and clearly state assumptions required for each interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report sensitivity to surface condition and preparation
rubrics_metrics.description: Noted that prism B produced no orders of colours even when newly ground and polished; surface condition and polish affect observations and must be reported.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe sample preparation and surface condition (polish, grinding), and report how such factors influenced results. Discuss reproducibility across different surface treatments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide detailed tabulated data for reproducibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Tables list angles of incidence, colours/tints, names of oils, images at prism surfaces, and notes on temperature effects—data supporting claims are recorded in tabular form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include comprehensive tables of measured quantities and observational notes (angles, tints, material IDs, temperatures). This supports reproducibility and independent verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derive conclusions directly supported by experimental evidence and state scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Conclusions drawn: reflective and refractive forces in media of same refractive power do not follow same law; reflective force varies according to different laws in different bodies; refracting forces may similarly vary—these are tied to experimental observations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure that high-level conclusions follow from the presented data. State the domain and limits (which materials, angles, wavelengths) over which conclusions are claimed to hold, and avoid overgeneralization beyond the tested conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alert to insidious fallacies in multivalued-function reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: A very insidious species of fallacy can intrude in reasoning about multivalued functions; vigilance is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly identify potential logical pitfalls (hidden assumptions about value selection, branch-cut inconsistencies). Where multivaluedness exists, track choices rigorously and warn readers of common missteps.
